## Why the method exists {#sec-coint-why}

Log house prices and log income in a state both wander: each has a **unit
root**, a shock that never fades, so neither returns to a fixed level
([why it matters](index.qmd#sec-ur-why)). Regress one on the other and the
fit looks good. It would look good for any two wandering series, related or
not. That is the **spurious regression**, noticed in the 1920s and shown by
Monte Carlo in the 1970s: a confident *t* statistic between two series that
have nothing to do with each other [@granger1974; @pesaran2015, p. 26].

What rescues the regression is its residual. If prices and income share one
trend, the gap between them does not wander: it is stationary, and the slope
is a long-run elasticity. Two series that are each I(1), integrated of order
one, stationary only after differencing, but have a stationary linear
combination are **cointegrated** [@engle1987; @pesaran2015, p. 523]. The
test is to regress, take the residual, and test it for a unit root
[@engle1987; @pesaran2015, p. 525]. In one state over 29 years that test has
almost no power: cointegration tests on a single series are weak at short
*T* [@baltagi2021, p. 357], for the same reason the unit-root tests of
[the unit-root note](theory-panel-unit-roots.qmd) are.

So the panel is pooled for power, and the proviso of that note returns: the
states must bring independent evidence. The panel also adds a trap of its
own. Stack *N* independent spurious regressions, and the pooled slope no
longer wanders as a single spurious slope does: it converges to a long-run
average, with a normal limit, whether or not any cointegration exists
[@phillips1999; @baltagi2021, p. 355]. Its *t* statistic still grows with
$\sqrt T$, so the tendency to find a relation that is not there "may be even
stronger in panel data regressions than in the pure time series case"
[@kao1999; @pesaran2015, p. 844]. A sensible pooled slope is no evidence of a
long-run relation. Only the residual is.

## One unit: a regression and a rank {#sec-coint-one-unit}

Write the **cointegrating regression** of state *i* as

$$y_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta_i x_{it} + u_{it},$$

with $y$ log price and $x$ log income. The Engle–Granger test runs OLS, then
a Dickey–Fuller regression on $\hat u_{it}$ with no intercept and no trend; a
rejection of the unit root is read as cointegration [@engle1987;
@pesaran2015, p. 525]. The critical values are not those of a unit-root test
on an observed series. Under the null the regression is spurious, so the
residual has a distribution of its own, tabulated for it [@phillips1990;
@pesaran2015, p. 525]. The result also depends on which series is on the
left, and the test can see at most one relation [@pesaran2015,
pp. 525–526].

Johansen's test removes both limits by treating the pair as a system. Stack
$z_{it} = (y_{it}, x_{it})'$ and write its vector autoregression in error
correction form,

$$\Delta z_{it} = \Pi_i z_{i,t-1}
  + \sum_{j=1}^{p-1} \Gamma_{ij} \Delta z_{i,t-j} + u_{it},
  \qquad \Pi_i = \alpha_i \beta_i'.$$

If $z_{it}$ is I(1), the left side and the lagged differences are
stationary, so $\Pi_i z_{i,t-1}$ must be too, and that forces $\Pi_i$ to
have reduced rank. The **rank** $r_i$ of $\Pi_i$ is the number of stationary
combinations, and $\beta_i$ holds them [@johansen1988; @johansen1991;
@pesaran2015, p. 529]. With two series, $r_i = 0$ means no shared trend,
$r_i = 1$ one shared trend, and $r_i = 2$ that both series are stationary,
which contradicts the unit-root result the chapter started from. The
**trace statistic** for rank $r$ against rank $m$ is

$$\mathrm{LR}(H_r \mid H_m) = -T \sum_{i=r+1}^{m} \log(1 - \hat\lambda_i),$$

built from the smallest eigenvalues of the reduced-rank regression, and it
does not change when the series are reordered [@johansen1991; @pesaran2015,
p. 541]. Its limit is a multivariate Dickey–Fuller distribution, with
critical values that depend on the number of series and on whether the
constant and trend are restricted to the long-run relation or left free
[@pesaran2015, p. 543]. That choice is Johansen's five cases [@johansen1994;
@pesaran2015, p. 539]; the step's default, an unrestricted constant and no
trend, is the third case, which allows a drift in the levels. The whole
apparatus is asymptotic, and Monte Carlo evidence says it is reliable only
when *T* is reasonably large and the system small [@pesaran2015, p. 547].
At $T = 29$ per state, the step's 49 ranks are a tally, not 49 verdicts.

## The precondition {#sec-coint-precondition}

The panel tests below are residual tests. @pesaran2015 [p. 839] states the
condition under which a residual test is the right tool: $r_i = 1$ in every
unit, with the variables split as $(y_{it}, x_{it}')$ and no cointegration
among the regressors $x_{it}$. A system test allows $r_i > 1$ and needs no
such split. The two also treat the residual's serial correlation
differently. Residual tests absorb it in a **long-run variance**, the
variance a serially correlated series shows in its running sums, estimated
without a model; system tests model it with the VAR's lags [@pesaran2015,
p. 839]. With one regressor the second half of the condition holds by
default, and the first half is what the state-by-state ranks check.

The single-equation estimators of the long run share the condition. All
regressors must be I(1) and not cointegrated among themselves, or the
long-run variance matrix they divide by is singular; and the relation must
be one that $y_{it}$ truly enters, since it is normalised to a unit
coefficient [@pesaran2015, p. 852].

Why not one system for the whole panel? Stack every state's pair into one
vector and run Johansen on it, and cointegration within states and across
them is covered at once, with a free error covariance for the dependence.
That works when the stacked vector has fewer than about ten series and
$T > 100$ [@banerjee2004; @pesaran2015, pp. 839–840]; the number of
parameters grows with $N^2$, so *T* must be far larger than *N*
[@pesaran2015, p. 855]. At 98 series and $T = 29$ it is out of reach. In
practice the dependence is carried by **common factors**, a few unobserved
series that load on every unit, each to its own degree ([common factors and
CCE](../02-cross-dependence/theory-common-factors-cce.qmd)). That is the
setting of equation 31.38 in @pesaran2015 [p. 840], and it is where the
substitute below comes from.

## Four panel tests {#sec-coint-tests}

**Kao.** One slope for every unit, and the error tested for a unit root with
the panel pooled. Take the **within residuals** $\tilde e_{it}$, the
residuals of the fit with a state intercept
([fixed or random](../05-core/index.qmd#sec-core-fe-re)), and run

$$\tilde e_{it} = \rho \tilde e_{i,t-1} + v_{it}.$$

The null of no cointegration is $\rho = 1$ [@kao1999; @baltagi2021, p. 357].
Kao builds four Dickey–Fuller statistics from $\hat\rho$ and its *t* ratio,
two for regressors unrelated to the error at every date and two allowing the
regressors and the error to be related, plus an ADF statistic from the
lag-augmented regression. Each is shifted and scaled by a mean and variance
and converges to $N(0, 1)$ in sequential limits, *T* first and then *N*
[@kao1999; @baltagi2021, pp. 357–358; @pesaran2015, p. 848]. The correction
assumes the nuisance parameters are the same for every unit [@pesaran2015,
p. 848].

**McCoskey–Kao.** The reverse null. With unit-specific slopes, the error is
split into a random walk and a noise term, and the null of cointegration is
that the random walk has zero variance. The statistic is the LM form

$$\mathrm{LM} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{1}{T^2}
  \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{S_{it}^2}{\hat\sigma_e^2},
  \qquad S_{it} = \sum_{j=1}^{t} \hat e_{ij},$$

a partial sum of residuals, and $\sqrt N (\mathrm{LM} - \mu) \to N(0,
\sigma^2)$ with moments found by simulation [@mccoskey1998; @baltagi2021,
p. 359]. The residuals must come from an efficient estimator of the long run
[@baltagi2021, p. 359], and the test is the panel version of the
single-series test of a stationary error [@pesaran2015, p. 850]. Two
warnings come with it: the asymptotic approximation is often poor, and the
test "is not equipped to deal with cross-sectional dependence"
[@baltagi2021, p. 359].

**Pedroni.** Unit-specific slopes, and seven statistics in two families
[@pedroni1999; @pedroni2004]. The **group-mean** family computes a statistic
unit by unit and averages, as a unit-root test against a heterogeneous
alternative does; the **panel** family sums numerator and denominator over
units before dividing, as a test against one common alternative does
[@baltagi2021, p. 360; @pesaran2015, pp. 848–849]. @baltagi2021
[pp. 360–361, eqs. 12.25–12.26] prints one of each. The group-mean $\rho$
form is a sum of unit-by-unit Phillips–Ouliaris statistics,

$$Z_{\tilde\rho} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}
  \frac{\sum_{t}(\hat e_{i,t-1}\Delta\hat e_{it} - \hat\lambda_i)}
       {\sum_{t}\hat e_{i,t-1}^2},$$

with $\hat\lambda_i$ half the gap between the long-run and the
contemporaneous variance of unit *i*'s residual; the panel *t* form sums
over units first, each unit weighted by its long-run conditional variance.
Each statistic is read after centring and scaling by tabulated moments,
$(Z - \mu\sqrt N)/\sigma \to N(0, 1)$ [@pedroni1999; @pesaran2015, p. 849];
for the model with an intercept and no trend, the panel *t* form obeys
$Z_{\hat t} + 1.73\sqrt N \to N(0, 0.93)$ [@baltagi2021, p. 361]. Averaging
pieces rather than whole statistics makes a rejection hard to read; the
averaged statistics have the plain reading, that enough units sit far from
what the null predicts [@baltagi2021, p. 361].

**Larsson–Lyhagen–Löthgren.** The system test. Run Johansen's trace test in
each unit, centre and scale each statistic by its tabulated mean and
variance, and average. The LR-bar statistic is IPS, the mean of
unit-by-unit statistics ([first-generation
tests](index.qmd#sec-ur-first-gen)), applied to trace statistics instead
of ADF *t* ratios, and it is asymptotically $N(0, 1)$ [@larsson2001;
@baltagi2021, p. 361; @pesaran2015, pp. 849–850]. It tests no cointegration
in any unit against at most $r_0 \ge 1$ relations, and unlike the residual
tests it allows more than one relation per unit; the moments are tabulated
for the model without deterministic terms by @larsson2001 and with a
constant and trend by @breitung2005 [@pesaran2015, p. 850]. It needs a large
*T*: with a short *T* the size is severely distorted however large *N* is
[@baltagi2021, p. 361].

## Dependence {#sec-coint-dependence}

The unit-root note ends on [the assumption no test
checks](theory-panel-unit-roots.qmd): units may share a trend, and the
[traps step](index.qmd#sec-ur-cross-coint) shows that no correlation
statistic sees it. For cointegration tests the consequence is stated
outright. The literature assumes one cointegrating vector per unit and lets
units depend on each other only through short-run dynamics; when units are
cointegrated with each other, "both univariate and multivariate panel
cointegration tests can be substantially over-sized" [@banerjee2004;
@baltagi2021, p. 362]. The remedy proposed is to extract each unit's common
trend by Johansen's method and test for cointegration among the trends
[@baltagi2021, p. 362], a procedure demonstrated on panels of at most eight
units [@pesaran2015, p. 843].

A common factor is the gentler case, and it is enough to break the tests.
Under the factor structure of @bai2004, Kao's and Pedroni's statistics are
no longer asymptotically normal and converge at the rate $T$ rather than
$\sqrt N T$; the remedy is to estimate the factors, strip them from the
data, and test the defactored residuals [@gengenbach2006; @baltagi2021,
p. 362]. On the unit-root side, PANIC, the test that defactors by principal
components and tests factors and remainders separately, is invalid in its
pooled form: replacing the remainders by estimates biases the pooled
statistic, and @bai2010 supply an alternative [@westerlund2009;
@pesaran2015, p. 837]. Pesaran's verdict on the field is that "a general
approach that is capable of addressing all the various issues involved does
not exist if *N* is relatively large" [@pesaran2015, p. 843].

## Long-run estimation {#sec-coint-estimation}

Once the residual is stationary, the slope is the long-run elasticity, and
the question is how to estimate it. OLS on a cointegrated panel is
consistent at rate $T\sqrt N$, so the years do more than the states, but
with regressors that respond to the error it is inefficient [@pesaran2015,
p. 850]. Two corrections share the field.

**FMOLS** adjusts the dependent variable for the part of the error that is
correlated with the regressor's innovations and subtracts a bias term from
the cross product, both built from non-parametric long-run variances
[@phillips1999; @pedroni2000; @pesaran2015, pp. 850–851, eqs. 31.51–31.52].
**DOLS** does the same by regression: add leads and lags of $\Delta x_{it}$
to the cointegrating regression, so that what is left is orthogonal to the
regressor's past and future [@kao2000; @pesaran2015, p. 851,
eqs. 31.53–31.54]. The two have the same limiting distribution,

$$T\sqrt N\,(\hat\beta - \beta) \to
  N\!\left(0,\; 6\,\Omega_\varepsilon^{-1}
  \sigma^2_{u \mid \varepsilon}\right)$$

in the homogeneous case [@kao2000; @pesaran2015, p. 851]. Both maintain
cross-sectional independence [@baltagi2021, p. 364]. Both also rest on
kernel estimates of long-run variances, which perform poorly when *T* is
under 20 [@pesaran2015, p. 851]. Breitung's two-step estimator, which fits
the short-run and long-run parameters separately, has a smaller small-sample
bias and more reliable standard errors than either in his experiments
[@breitung2005; @pesaran2015, p. 853]; in the large simulation of
@wagner2010, DOLS beats every other estimator, with FMOLS and the two-step
estimator similar [@pesaran2015, p. 853].

**Under dependence.** Three estimators relax independence, and all three
represent it as a correlation between the units' errors at the same date.
**DSUR** is a GLS fit of the DOLS regression, OLS after reweighting by the
long-run error covariance across units, for one homogeneous cointegrating
vector [@mark2005; @moon2005; @pesaran2015, pp. 853–854, eq. 31.57].
Bai–Kao and Westerlund add stationary common factors to the error and run
FMOLS around them; Bai–Kao–Ng allow non-stationary factors and estimate
slope, factors and loadings by iterating on a least-squares criterion, with
a bias correction [@bai2006kao; @westerlund2007factors; @bai2009kao;
@pesaran2015, p. 854, eqs. 31.58–31.59]. None of them allows cross-unit
cointegration [@pesaran2015, p. 854]. The panel VECM that would, Johansen
on the stacked vector, is the infeasible system of the precondition section
[@groen2003; @pesaran2015, pp. 854–855, eq. 31.60].

**The substitute the book runs.** None of the above is in R. What is in R
is **CCE**, the regression that adds cross-state averages of price and
income to each state's equation to stand in for the common factors
([CCE](../02-cross-dependence/index.qmd#sec-cce)). Its estimates are
consistent whether the factors are stationary, non-stationary or
cointegrated, so long as the idiosyncratic error is stationary and the
number of factors fixed [@kapetanios2011; @pesaran2015, p. 845]. On these 49
states @holly2010 report CCEMG and CCEP slopes of 1.14 (0.20) and 1.20
(0.21), do not reject a unit elasticity, and test the gap $p_{it} - y_{it}$
with **CIPS**, the panel unit-root test that defactors with the same
averages ([second-generation tests](index.qmd#sec-ur-second-gen)):
statistics of −2.16 to −2.45 against a 5% value of −2.11, read as
cointegration "for a sufficiently large number of States" [@pesaran2015,
pp. 845–846]. @croissant2019 [p. 209] shorten the route and run CIPS
directly on the CCE residuals, with no deterministic term because the fit
already carries one, and conclude that both CCE fits "represent
cointegrating regressions".

The book runs the second version and labels it a substitute, for two
reasons. The CIPS critical values are those of a unit-root test on an
observed series; the single-series literature shows that a residual has a
distribution of its own, which is why Engle–Granger has its own tables
[@pesaran2015, p. 525]. @holly2010 avoid the problem by fixing the slope at
one before testing; the residual version does not. And CIPS tests the
alternative that a *share* of units has a stationary residual ([what a
rejection means](index.qmd#sec-ur-alternative)), so a rejection says that
enough states' gaps revert, not that every state's does. What the substitute
keeps is the one thing the estimators above lack: it allows the common shock
that the [CD test](../02-cross-dependence/index.qmd#sec-csd-tests), the
test of whether units move together, found in every state.

## Finite samples {#sec-coint-finite}

Two Monte Carlo studies set expectations for $T = 29$. @gutierrez2003 finds
that at $T = 10$ Kao's tests have more power than Pedroni's, and still
little even at $N = 100$; at large *T* Pedroni's win; both beat the LR-bar.
The danger runs both ways: with a long panel the whole panel is called
cointegrated when a small fraction of units is, and with a short one it is
called not cointegrated when a large fraction is [@gutierrez2003;
@baltagi2021, p. 363]. @wagner2010 cover the single-equation and the system
tests at once. Two of Pedroni's statistics, the ADF-based ones, perform
best; every other test is severely undersized with low power, "dismal for
$T \le 25$"; Pedroni's are also the least affected by short-run dependence
or cross-unit cointegration; and the system tests are very bad at small *T*
and unreliable for the rank [@wagner2010; @baltagi2021, p. 363;
@pesaran2015, p. 849].

The project's own check, in the Pitfalls of the [cointegration
step](index.qmd#sec-ur-coint), is of the implementation rather than the
tests. At $N = 49$, $T = 29$, the five scale-free statistics as computed
there reject in almost none of 200 draws without cointegration and in all
200 with it, and the other two change with the units of measurement, which
Pedroni's statistics cannot. They separate the hypotheses and fail the
$N(0, 1)$ calibration, so the step reports them as unverified.

## If / then {#sec-coint-if-then}

| If | Then |
|---|---|
| Both series fail to reject a unit root, state by state and as a panel | Test the residual before reading any slope: a pooled slope converges even with no cointegration [@phillips1999; @baltagi2021, p. 355]. |
| A unit's Johansen rank is 2 | One of its series is stationary; the residual tests' precondition $r_i = 1$ fails there [@pesaran2015, p. 839]. |
| Johansen's rank is read at $T \approx 30$ | Report the tally, not the verdicts: the trace test is asymptotic and needs a reasonably large *T* [@pesaran2015, p. 547]. |
| The CD test rejects on the residuals | Kao, McCoskey–Kao and Pedroni lose their normal limits; defactor first [@gengenbach2006; @baltagi2021, p. 362]. |
| Units may share a trend | Every test above is over-sized; test the common trends for cointegration among themselves [@banerjee2004; @baltagi2021, p. 362]. |
| $T \le 25$ | Expect low power from every residual test, and do not trust a system test's rank [@wagner2010; @baltagi2021, p. 363]. |
| The slope is wanted and units are independent | DOLS, then FMOLS; both need *T* well above 20 for the long-run variances [@wagner2010; @pesaran2015, pp. 851, 853]. |
| The slope is wanted and units share a factor | DSUR, Bai–Kao or Bai–Kao–Ng in principle; CCE with CIPS on its residual in this book, labelled a substitute [@pesaran2015, p. 854; @croissant2019, p. 209]. |
| CIPS rejects on the CCE residual | A share of states' price–income gaps revert; say "a share", and say the critical values are those of a unit-root test [@pesaran2015, p. 525]. |

## Open {#sec-coint-open}

- **No implementation.** Kao, McCoskey–Kao, Larsson–Lyhagen–Löthgren,
  Westerlund's error-correction tests [@westerlund2007], FMOLS, DOLS, DSUR
  and the factor estimators have no R implementation in this project. The
  Stata benchmarks, `xtcointtest kao`, `xtcointtest pedroni` and
  `xtcointtest westerlund`, are deferred to a later plan.
- **`pco`.** The only Pedroni implementation is archived on CRAN, two of its
  seven statistics depend on the units of measurement, and the moments it
  standardises with cannot be checked against Table 2 of @pedroni1999,
  which is not in `lit/`. Its five remaining statistics are reported
  unverified.
- **The precondition at $T = 29$.** $r_i = 1$ cannot be confirmed state by
  state; the tally of ranks is the evidence.
- **The substitute's critical values.** CIPS on a regression residual reads
  unit-root tables. No panel residual-based table exists for it, and this
  book does not simulate one.
- **Baltagi's targets.** Tables 12.3 to 12.7 of @baltagi2021 run Kao,
  Pedroni, FMOLS and DOLS on the R&D panel of @kao1999rd, which ships in no
  R package. They are not reproduced.
